Westmoreland Resources. To date the submitted reclamation plans have called for a high level of reclamation. Westmoreland Resources recognizes the fact that technology and regulations concerning reclamation are constantly changing and is prepared to make any required changes that will improve reclamation success.
Less stringent reclamation plans would result in greater environmental impacts to the land and people. These could include less vegetation on reclaimed land, pollution of surface and ground-water, permanent disruption of drainage patterns, serious erosion, and aesthetic damage.
The economic terms of the leases have been negotiated by the Tribe and approved by the Department of the Interior. These negotiations resulted in royalty rates stated as a percentage of the FOB mine price and minimum production levels with penalties for failure to meet those levels. The royalty rate is renegotiable each ten years. Because the royalty rate is a percentage of the sales price, the Crow Tribe will share in the expected future inflation in the value of the coal. Whether this income would be used by the Tribe to limit the negative social impacts by expansion of local services depends on what use the Tribe makes of such income. Any increase in the percentage royalty may have an adverse effect on the ability of the lessee to competitively sell coal produced from these leases, and consequently on Tribal job opportunities and Tribal revenues.
<u>Deferred Development</u> - The Crow Tribe and/or the Secretary of the Interior could choose to stretch development over a longer time period by deferring further coal development upon the leases until adequate and effective land use and community development controls are implemented.
